d: Pathologically excessive (and often incoherent) talking
r: Logo- “word; speech” + -rrhea “flowing”
s: A volubility sometimes amounting to a logorrhœa in expressing what they know.
old_f: Excessively careful (and often pointless) reasoning
Compulsively frequent (and often secret) writing
Chronically damaged (and often swollen) eyelids
ety: From logo- (prefix meaning ‘word; speech’) + -rrhea (suffix meaning ‘flowing’), probably modelled after verbal diarrhea. logo- is derived from Ancient Greek λόγος (lógos, “word; speech; utterance”) (from λέγω (légō, “to say, speak; to arrange; to gather”), from Proto-Indo-European *leǵ- (“to collect, gather”)), while -rrhea is from ῥοία (rhoía, “a flow, flux”) (from ῥέω (rhéō, “to flow”), from Proto-Indo-European *srew- (“to flow”)).

d: Adapted for grasping especially by wrapping around an object
r: Latin prehēnsus, from prehendō “grasp, seize”
s: Some monkeys have prehensile tails which they use to pick things up.
old_f: Adapted for digging especially by scraping with broad flat feet
Adapted for swimming especially by paddling with webbed toes
Adapted for warning especially by producing a loud rattle
ety: Borrowed from French préhensile, from Latin perfect passive participle prehēnsus, from prehendō (“grasp, seize”) + adjective suffix -ile, from Latin -ilis.

d: Someone who intrudes on the privacy or property of another without permission
r: Inter- + loper “runner, rover”
s: They disliked the interloper, and forced him to leave.
old_f: Someone who carries messages between two parties who refuse to meet in person
Someone who runs away with a partner in order to marry without consent
Someone who measures land and marks its boundaries for a title deed
ety: From inter- + loper (“runner, rover”), as in landloper (“vagrant”) (from lope (“to leap, to jump”) (originally dialectal)). Originally spelt enterloper and used in specific sense, “unauthorized trader trespassing on privileges of chartered companies”, later general sense of “self-interested intruder” from 1630s.

d: An assistant or subordinate bishop of a diocese
r: Old French suffragan, from Latin suffrāgium “suffrage”
s: A suffragan could share the tasks which were special to bishops; for example, by conducting confirmations.
old_f: A woman who campaigned for the right to vote
A long hymn sung on days of fasting
A minor clerk who keeps parish records
ety: From Anglo-Norman, Old French suffragam, from (the stem of) Latin suffrāgium (“suffrage”).

d: Lying on the stomach with head raised with legs pointed forward
r: Middle French couchant
s: Have you ever watched fine collie dogs couchant at twenty yards' distance?
old_f: Standing on the hind legs with forepaws raised as if to strike
Walking with the right forepaw raised and head turned to face the viewer
Sitting upright on the haunches with the tail curled around the feet
ety: From Middle English couchant, from Middle French couchant.

d: Cause to be more favorably inclined; gain the good will of
r: Late Latin mollificō, from Latin mollis “soft”
s: He tried to mollify the angry customer.
old_f: Cause to grow mold or decay; spoil by leaving in damp
Grind into a fine powder; crush with a pestle
Shape in a mold or cast; form from soft clay
ety: From Middle English mollifien, from Late Latin mollificō, from Latin mollis (“soft”). By surface analysis, Latin moll- + -ify.

d: Associated by chance and not an integral part
r: Medieval Latin adventītius “coming from abroad, extraneous”, from Latin adventus “arrival”
s: The adventitious disappearance of those nearer the throne than the duke had, moreover, set tongues awagging.
old_f: Eager for new experiences and not afraid of danger
Arriving in time for a holiday and not a moment late
Useful for some purpose and not just decoration
ety: From Medieval Latin adventītius (“coming from abroad, extraneous”), a corruption of Latin adventīcius (“foreign, strange, accidental”), from adventus (“arrival, coming, approach, advent”) + -īcius (suffix forming adjectives), from adveniō (“to arrive”) + -tus (suffix forming action nouns).

d: Stop from happening or developing
r: Origin uncertain; possibly a variant of kurbash “heavy whip, lash”
s: An Allied mission to kibosh the German A-bomb.
old_f: Chat idly with neighbors
Cook slowly on a skewer
Wrap tightly in cloth
ety: The origin of the noun is uncertain; the following etymologies have been suggested: * According to Gerald Leonard Cohen, Stephen Goranson, and Matthew Little, at present the most likely derivation is as a non-rhotic variant of kurbash (“heavy whip, lash”), from Arabic كُرْبَاج (kurbāj, “lash, whip”), or from its etymon Ottoman Turkish قرباچ (kırbaç, “lash, whip”) (whence Turkish kırbaç (“whip”)). * From Irish caidhp bháis (literally “death cap”), said to denote, among other things, the black cap worn by English judges when pronouncing the death sentence, the hood put on a person before they we

d: Feelings of anxiety that make you tense and irritable
r: Dis- + quietude
s: The lawyer stood awhile when Mr. Hyde had left him, the picture of disquietude.
old_f: Feelings of disgust that make you turn away from food
Feelings of contentment that come after long hard work
Feelings of loneliness that come from living in silence
ety: From dis- + quietude.

d: Possessing or believed to possess magic power especially protective power
r: Talisman + -ic
s: For Marshall, law possessed a talismanic quality, representing all that was best in American democracy.
old_f: Possessing or claiming to possess great skill especially in storytelling
Relating to or made of soft white clay especially for medicine
Tending to or inclined to gossip especially about neighbors
ety: From talisman + -ic.

d: Someone who lends money at excessive rates of interest
r: Old French usurier, from Latin ūsūra “interest”
s: You can go to the Carpetbag usurers if you want money.
old_f: Someone who seizes a throne without any rightful claim to it
Someone who guides guests to their seats at a theatre
Someone who repairs worn-out tools and household goods for resale
ety: Anglo-Norman, from Old French usurier, Latin ūsūra (“interest”).

d: A rope for raising or lowering a sail or flag
r: Middle English halier, from halen “to haul”, later confused with yard
s: Uncleat the black main halyard to lower and remove the jib cover.
old_f: A pole for measuring the depth of a channel or harbor
A yard of land set aside for grazing horses or cattle
A hook for hauling fish or nets onto a boat
ety: Inherited from Middle English halier, from halen (“to haul”) + -iere (“-er”), with misconstrual of -ier as yard. Compare lanyard.

d: State of disgrace resulting from public abuse
r: Late Latin obloquium “contradiction”, from Latin obloquor “speak against”
s: The death of her honour has added obloquy and shame to that sorrow which bends my grey hairs to the dust!
old_f: A slanting line used in writing
A formal speech praising the dead
A duty imposed by law or custom
ety: From Middle English obloqui, obloquie, obloquy, from Middle French obloquie and its etymon Late Latin obloquium (“contradiction”), from Latin obloquor (“speak against, contradict”). By surface analysis, ob- + -loquy.

d: Rich and superior in quality
r: Latin opulēns, from ops “wealth, power, resources”
s: Bowed into the opulent suites of Ritzes and Waldorfs.
old_f: Open and easy to reach
Thick and cloudy
Hopeful about the future
ety: Borrowed from Latin opulēns, opulentus, from ops (“wealth, power, resources”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃op- (“to work; produce in abundance”).

d: The floating wreckage of a ship
r: Anglo-Norman floteson, from Old French flotaison “a floating”
s: That gaggle of human flotsam doesn't even belong on the sea.
old_f: The loose sand on a riverbed
The small boats of a fleet
The froth that forms on beer
ety: From Anglo-Norman floteson, from Old French flotaison (“a floating”), from floter (“to float”), of Germanic origin (See float.), + -aison, from Latin -atio.

d: Rope or canvas headgear for a horse, with a rope for leading
r: Perhaps Spanish jáquima “halter”
s: He’d hauled the horse around by the hackamore and was pounding off up the track.
old_f: Iron or wooden frame for a saddle, with a horn for roping
Leather or felt pad for a horse, with a pocket for oats
Clay or stone trough for a stable, with a spout for draining
ety: Perhaps from Spanish jáquima (“halter”).

d: Light carriage; pulled by a single horse
r: Named after the British statesman Lord Brougham (1778–1868)
s: “A nice little brougham and a pair of beauties.”
old_f: Rough broom; made of a single bundle of twigs
Thick broth; made with a single kind of meat
Heavy boot; worn by a single class of laborer
ety: Named after British statesman Lord Brougham (1778–1868), who either invented or popularized the vehicle.

d: The effect of supernatural or divine intervention in human affairs
r: Greek theourgíā “sorcery”, from theós “god” + érgon “work”
s: Spiritual magic or theurgy was based on the idea that one could reach God in an ascent up the scale of creation.
old_f: The theory that all matter is made of a single substance
The sense of urgency that drives prophets to preach in public
The practice of composing hymns for performance at religious festivals
ety: From Late Latin theūrgia, from Ancient Greek θεουργίᾱ (theourgíā, “sorcery”), from θεός (theós, “god”) + ἔργον (érgon, “work”). By surface analysis, the- + -urgy.

d: Quickly aroused to anger
r: Late Latin īrāscibilis, from Latin īrāscī “to be angry, enraged”
s: I am naturally irascible, and if I could have shaken this negative gentleman vigorously, the relief would have been immense.
old_f: Easily erased or removed
Reckless and impulsive
Bright with rainbow colors
ety: From Middle English, from Old French irascible, from Late Latin īrāscibilis, from Latin īrāscī (“to be angry, enraged”) + -bilis. See also -ible.

d: A camp defended by a circular formation of wagons
r: South African Dutch lager “camp”, from German Lager; a doublet of lager and lair
s: Then our frontiers will shrink as we draw our little laager more and more tightly.
old_f: A pale beer brewed and stored at low temperatures
A wide flat field flooded for growing rice
A small cart drawn by a pair of dogs
ety: From South African Dutch lager (“camp”) (modern Afrikaans laer), from German Lager, from Middle High German leger, from Old High German legar, from Proto-Germanic *legrą. Doublet of lager and lair.

d: A garment resembling a tunic that was worn by men in the Middle Ages
r: Old English cyrtel; compare Old Norse kyrtill “tunic”
s: Many of the church dignitaries are distinguishable by peculiarities of dress, as the shovel hat and kirtle.
old_f: A small round shield that was carried by foot soldiers in the Middle Ages
A shallow iron pot that was used for cooking over open fires in the Middle Ages
A narrow strip of land that was farmed by peasants in the Middle Ages
ety: From Middle English kirtel, from Old English cyrtel, cognate with Old Norse kyrtill (“tunic”) (whence Icelandic kyrtill, Danish kjortel (“gown, tunic”), Swedish kjortel (“petticoat, skirt”)), from Old Norse *kurtil-, supposedly a diminutive of *kurt-, from Latin curtus (“short, shortened”). Compare German Kittel.

d: A conspicuous mistake whose effects seem to reverberate
r: Clang “loud ringing sound” + -er
s: In his speech, the best man got the bride's name wrong. What a clanger!
old_f: A large brass bell rung to call workers home
A member of a powerful family group
A metal latch on a farm gate
ety: From clang (“loud ringing sound”) + -er.

d: Translating an idea into action
r: Greek prâxis “action, activity, practice”
s: Differences between theory and praxis of communism.
old_f: Reading a meaning into dreams
Planning a route before travel
Comparing a text with its source
ety: Partly from Latin prāxis and partly from its etymon Ancient Greek πρᾶξις (prâxis, “action, activity, practice”).

d: Resembling or characteristic of a prophet or prophecy
r: Latin sibyllinus, from Sibylla; sibyl + -ine
s: Another early form of rhapsodomancy is represented by the sibylline books.
old_f: Resembling or characteristic of a brother or sister
Resembling or characteristic of a soft hissing sound
Resembling or characteristic of a pale silver metal
ety: From Latin sibyllinus, Sibillinus, from Sibylla. By surface analysis, sibyl + -ine.

d: Large deep serving dish with a cover; for serving soups and stews
r: French terrine; a doublet of terrine
s: The large covered soup tureen, as well as the 15 inch round plate on which it sat, was rimmed by gold leaf.
old_f: Small round cake with a crust; for eating at weddings and feasts
Tall narrow tower with a bell; for calling villagers to prayer
Thick woollen cloth with a twill; for making coats and cloaks
ety: From earlier terrene (thus pronunciations with /tj/, /t͡ʃ/ are spelling pronunciations), borrowed from French terrine. Doublet of terrine.

d: A person who walks from place to place
r: Greek peripatētikós “given to walking around”, from perí “around” + patéō “to walk”
s: He who would think clearly must think like a peripatetic even if he is unwilling to walk like one.
old_f: A person who speaks in roundabout phrases
A person who lives at the edge of a town
A person who preaches outdoors
ety: From French péripatétique, from Latin peripatēticus, from Ancient Greek περιπατητικός (peripatētikós, “given to walking around”), from περιπατέω (peripatéō, “to walk around”), from περί (perí, “around”) (English peri-)+ πατέω (patéō, “to walk”).

d: Contaminated with infecting organisms
r: Latin pestifer “bearing plague”, from pestis “plague” + -fer “carrying”
s: In these solemn moments man discovers the germ of those vices, which like the Java tree shed a pestiferous vapour around.
old_f: Prone to constant nagging
Ground into a paste
Ripe with summer fruit
ety: Mid 15th century, in sense “mischievous, pernicious”, from Latin pestifer (“bearing plague”), from pestis (“plague”) + -fer (“carrying”). By surface analysis, pesti- + -ferous (“bearing, carrying”).

d: Substituting a more inclusive term for a less inclusive one or vice versa
r: Greek sunekdokhḗ “receiving together”, from sún “with” + ek “out of” + dékhesthai “to accept”
s: "Holocaust" can become a tired synecdoche for war crimes in general.
old_f: Repeating the same sound at the start of several words in a line or phrase
Placing two words of opposite meaning side by side for dramatic effect
Describing something by stating what it is not in order to emphasize it
ety: Borrowed from Latin synecdochē, from Ancient Greek συνεκδοχή (sunekdokhḗ, “receiving together”) from σύν (sún, “with”) + ἐκ (ek, “out of”) + δέχεσθαι (dékhesthai, “to accept”), this last element related to δοκέω (dokéō, “to think, suppose, seem”).

d: Spur on or encourage especially by cheers and shouts
r: Latin exhortārī “to encourage”, from ex- + hortārī “to incite, spur”
s: And now, my dear sir, let me exhort you to take care of yourself.
old_f: Shorten or cut off especially by trimming the ends
Breathe out or release especially by sighing heavily
Dig up or remove especially by digging around the roots
ety: From Middle English exorten, from Old French exhorter, from Latin exhortārī (“to encourage”), from ex- (“out of, from”) + hortārī (“to incite, spur”).

d: Having a difficult and contrary disposition
r: Crotchet + -y, using crotchet in its 16th-century sense of a whim or fancy
s: So why is the comedian, actor and Observer columnist still so crotchety?
old_f: Having a crooked or zigzag shape
Having a habit of knitting or sewing
Having a short, stout build
ety: From crotchet + -y, using crotchet in the 16th-century sense of a whim or fancy.

d: The name by which a geographical place is known
r: Back-formation from toponymy: topo- + -nym
s: ‘Tangerine’ is a toponym of Tangier.
old_f: The highest point reached by a climber on a single expedition
The word that means the opposite of another word
The first title page of a printed book or pamphlet
ety: Back-formation from toponymy. By surface analysis, topo + -nym.

d: Earnest or urgent request
r: Entreat + -y
s: The entreaties of a lover and the rejection of the heroine lend charm to the stanza.
old_f: A formal peace agreement
A small decorative dish
A hidden entrance
ety: From entreat + -y.

d: A clown or buffoon (after the Harlequin character in the commedia dell’arte)
r: Middle French Harlequin, from Old French Hellequin, a demon or malevolent spirit
s: Motives are like harlequins—there is always a second dress beneath their first.
old_f: A herald or crier (after the trumpeters who announced the start of medieval tournaments)
A shepherd or herdsman (after the hero of a popular French pastoral romance)
A hunting horn or bugle (after the instruments carried by royal huntsmen)
ety: From earlier Harlicken, from Middle French Harlequin (in Italian Arlecchino, the name of a popular servant character in commedia dell'arte plays), from Old French Harlequin, Halequin, Herlequin, Hellequin, Hierlekin, Hellekin (a demon, malevolent spirit), probably of Germanic origin, connected to the Old English figure of *Herla Cyning (“King Herla”, a mythical figure identified with Woden) or possibly to Old Frisian helle kin, Old English helle cyn, Old Norse heljar kyn (“the kindred of Hell”). Related to Middle English Hurlewain (“a mischievous sprite or goblin”).

d: Excessively or hypocritically pious
r: Late Latin Pharisaicus + -al
s: The puritanical, pharisaical British conquered in the name of liberty and usurped under the cloak of altruism.
old_f: Relating to lighthouses
Relating to the throat
Relating to ancient kings
ety: From Late Latin Pharisaicus + -al.

d: Showing sustained enthusiastic action with unflagging vitality
r: Latin indēfatīgābilis “untiring”, from in- “not” + dēfatīgō “to tire out”
s: He was respected by all who knew him for his integrity and indefatigable attention to public business.
old_f: Showing no sign of fear when facing great danger
Lacking any clear or definite shape or outline
Impossible to beat or overcome in any contest
ety: From Middle French, from Latin indēfatīgābilis (“untiring”), from in- (“not”) + dēfatīgō (“to tire out”).

d: A roofed arcade or gallery with open sides stretching along the front or side of a building; often at an upper level
r: Italian loggia, from Old French loge; a doublet of lobby and lodge
s: Mr Carrados was standing in the loggia of the Hotel Beverley when a not unfamiliar sound claimed his attention.
old_f: A narrow wooden bridge with low rails crossing a stream at the bottom of a formal garden; often painted white
A tall clay jar with two handles used for storing olive oil in a cellar or pantry; often buried to the neck
A sunken stone basin with a carved spout set into a courtyard wall for washing hands; often fed by a spring
ety: Borrowed from Italian loggia, from Old French loge, from Medieval Latin laubĭa, from Frankish *laubijā. Doublet of lobby and lodge.

d: Hospital for persons with infectious diseases (especially leprosy)
r: Italian lazzaretto, from lazzaro “leper”, ultimately from the name Lazarus
s: It is probable that from their inception the lazaretti did not house all plague victims.
old_f: Chapel for prayers for the souls of the dead (especially in Venice)
Lodging for poor travelers on pilgrimage (especially to Rome)
Workshop for repairing ships and their rigging (especially oars)
ety: Borrowed from Italian lazzareto (archaic), lazzaretto, lazzeretto, from lazzaro (“leper”) + -etto (diminutive or meliorative suffix). Lazzaro is derived from Medieval Latin lazarus (“leper”), from Lazarus, from Ancient Greek Λᾱ́ζᾱρος (Lā́zāros), from Hebrew אֶלְעָזָר ('el'azár, literally “God has helped”), from אֵל ('él, “God; a deity, god”) + עָזַר ('azár, “to assist, help”). Lazarus is a Biblical character mentioned in the parable of Jesus known as “The rich man and Lazarus” who is described as being a beggar covered in sores: see Luke 16:20–21. Doublet of lazar and lazaret. The plural form

d: An unwholesome atmosphere
r: Greek míasma “stain; pollution”
s: It was into this lossy compression miasma that aptX was born.
old_f: A long sea voyage
A loud lament
A clouded mirror
ety: First attested in 1665. From Ancient Greek μίασμα (míasma, “stain; pollution”).

d: A lodge consisting of a frame covered with matting or brush; used by nomadic American Indians in the southwestern United States
r: Of uncertain source; similar words occur among several Native American peoples of the Southwest
s: A wickiup had been his bedroom, a blanket his robe.
old_f: A lamp consisting of a cotton cord floating in a bowl of oil; used by settlers in log cabins on the frontier of the United States
A game consisting of a hoop and stick thrown at a target; played by children at harvest gatherings in rural New England
A basket consisting of a willow frame lined with clay; used by early farmers to carry water in the dry plains of the West
ety: Wickiup-like structures were built by many Native American peoples throughout the Southwestern United States, and terms similar to wickiup are present "among Native Americans in Arizona, New Mexico, Utah, Idaho, and California", but the source of the word appears to be Fox wîkiyâpi (“house”). Alternatively, it may be a variant of wikiwam (“wigwam”). Either way, its ultimate origin is the Proto-Algonquian root *wi·kiwa·ʔmi (“house”). Doublet of wigwam.

d: Marked by unjust severity or arbitrary behavior
r: Latin tyrannus “tyrant” + -ous
s: Yield up, O love, thy crown and hearted throne To tyrannous hate!
old_f: Marked by deep wrinkles or creases
Marked by a fondness for practical jokes
Marked by loud and shrill singing
ety: From Latin tyrannus (“tyrant”) + English -ous.
